newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS - Czechs take steps to clean up capital mkts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Czechs take steps to clean up capital mkts.

text.p: The Czech government plans to open a new securities clearing house as part of a programme to build confidence in capital markets.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said on Thursday that the finance ministry would open a tender in February for an organisation to manage a clearing house.
Czech share trading has been criticised for years because of problems at the state-run Central Securities Registry (SCP).

"The finance ministry will call an open tender by the 15th of February for the opening of the clearing centre, so that a test operation can start by the end of this year and real operations at the beginning of 1998," Klaus told a news conference.
Speaking after s meeting with ministry staff about improving market supervision, Klaus said the new clearing house would not necessarily replace the SCP.
He did not elaborate on what criteria would be used for selecting the organisation to run the clearing house, or what might happen to the SCP.
Market participants welcomed the news as long as it ensured the end of the SCP's control over clearing.
"A lot of the complaints have been against the SCP," said Lubos Vystavel, chief equities trader at INB Barings in Prague.

Many investors, frustrated by cumbersome securities clearing and an absence of price quotes from the SCP where much of the over-the-counter trading is done, have called repeatedly for a better system to expedite trades.
Under the current system, payment is settled with the central bank, while share transfers are settled by the SCP.

In December, ministers agreed with capital market experts to move supervision of the securities' markets out of the finance ministry into a separate "Securities Bureau" which would evolve into an independent body akin to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

Prague Stock Exchange chairman Tomas Jezek is pushing for legislation which would alow a Czech SEC to be launched by July 1, as a way to bring more transparency to a securities market deemed by many to be opaque and ripe with insider trading.

But Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik, who has relunctantly agreed to move capital markets supervision into an independent body, said on Thursday that meeting Jezek's suggested schedule would be difficult.
Klaus said he was "satisfied with the strengthening of the activities of the (finance ministry) supervisor."
"It's been proven by the number of audits and sanctions during the last half year."
He said there was still "a lack of cooperation" between banking and capital market regulators, and interior ministry investigators, who are charged with uncovering financial crime.
